--- title: 'Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference' jupyter: python3 --- This is an executable companion to [OLS mathematics and Rust notes](../ols-math.qmd), for learning and reviewing the estimator. It uses Python to make the intermediate matrices visible; production estimation lives in `crates/stats-core/src/ols.rs`. NumPy and SciPy are notebook tools, not Rust dependencies. We use the same saved simulated housing observations as the PHP example and R fixtures. These are synthetic observations, not real housing records. We model $y=X\beta+\epsilon$. Rows are observations, columns are coefficients, and the first column is explicitly supplied ones. Our unknowns are the intercept and slope. We assume full column rank and $n>p$. Run cells from top to bottom; see [notebook setup](index.qmd). ::: {#7f44574b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path import json import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy.stats import t from IPython.display import Math, display def show_matrix(symbol, values): """Render calculated numbers as a LaTeX matrix, with its dimensions.""" matrix = np.asarray(values) if matrix.ndim == 1: matrix = matrix[:, None] rows = [" & ".join(f"{value:.6g}" for value in row) for row in matrix] latex = r"\begin{bmatrix}" + r" \\ ".join(rows) + r"\end{bmatrix}" display(Math(symbol + " = " + latex + rf"\quad({matrix.shape[0]}\times {matrix.shape[1]})")) def math_number(value): number = f"{value:.8g}" if "e" in number: mantissa, exponent = number.split("e") return mantissa + rf"\times10^{{{int(exponent)}}}" return number def show_dot(symbol, left, right): """Show the first two and last products, but sum every term.""" left, right = np.asarray(left), np.asarray(right) assert left.ndim == right.ndim == 1 and left.shape == right.shape terms = [rf"({math_number(a)})\cdot({math_number(b)})" for a, b in zip(left, right)] if len(terms) > 3: terms = terms[:2] + [r"\cdots", terms[-1]] display(Math(symbol + " = " + " + ".join(terms) + r"\approx " + math_number(left @ right))) # Run from the repository root or anywhere below it. ROOT = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "Cargo.toml").exists()) fixture = json.loads((ROOT / "tests/fixtures/ols-r.json").read_text()) case = next(c for c in fixture["cases"] if c["name"] == "simulated_housing") X = np.array(case["x"], dtype=float) y = np.array(case["y"], dtype=float) n, p = X.shape observations = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "docs/data/housing.csv") np.testing.assert_array_equal(X[:, 1], observations["area_m2"]) np.testing.assert_array_equal(y, observations["monthly_rent"]) display(observations) display(observations.corr().rename_axis("Sample Pearson correlations")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

area_m2 1.000000 0.961874 0.936149
bedrooms 0.961874 1.000000 0.932812
monthly_rent 0.936149 0.932812 1.000000
``` ::: ::: ### Where these data come from Each row is a simulated apartment: `area_m2` is floor area in square metres, `bedrooms` is a correlated count, and `monthly_rent` is rent in fictional currency units per month. The generator uses seed `20261011` and saves the eight observations in [housing.csv](../data/housing.csv). See `tests/generate-learning-data.R` for the complete generation process. The saved CSV, rather than independently generated samples in each language, is the input to every implementation. We generate area uniformly between 35 and 110 square metres, then generate bedrooms from area plus noise, rounded and bounded to 1–4. Rent follows $$\mathrm{rent}_i=650+18\,\mathrm{area}_i+\epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i\sim N(0,180^2).$$ So the population intercept is 650, the slope is 18 currency units per additional square metre, and the error standard deviation is 180. We know these because we wrote the simulation, not because an estimator discovered them. Estimated coefficients differ from the generating values because this sample contains noise. The correlation table above reports **observed sample Pearson correlations**. Area and rent are associated, as are area and bedroom count. Eight observations keep the matrices readable; they are a teaching sample, not enough to make reliable claims about a housing market. Correlation alone does not establish causation. The first model uses area only; bedrooms become a second predictor in the [verification notebook](ols-verification.qmd). Bedrooms have no additional direct term in this simulated rent equation, despite their correlation with rent. ### Read the matrices $X$ has $n=8$ rows (observations) and $p=2$ columns (intercept and slope). $y$ is a column vector, so its mathematical dimensions are $8\times1$. NumPy stores our vectors as one-dimensional arrays; we display them as columns. The second column contains the observed floor areas; the first column of ones is a constructed intercept column, not a measurement or a starting guess. The superscript $\top$ means **transpose**: swap rows and columns, without changing the values. In Python, `X.T` is $X^\top$. ::: {#8c0ffd37 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_matrix("X", X) show_matrix("y", y) show_matrix(r"X^\top", X.T) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 74.4 \\ 1 & 57.4 \\ 1 & 66.4 \\ 1 & 49.1 \\ 1 & 45.7 \\ 1 & 92.4 \\ 1 & 37 \\ 1 & 93.9\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle y = \begin{bmatrix}1879.25 \\ 1805.03 \\ 2022.29 \\ 1267.85 \\ 1509.24 \\ 2240.1 \\ 959.51 \\ 2386.54\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle X^\top = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 74.4 & 57.4 & 66.4 & 49.1 & 45.7 & 92.4 & 37 & 93.9\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 8)$ ::: ::: Matrix multiplication takes a row from the left matrix and a column from the right matrix, multiplies their corresponding entries, and adds the products. The inner dimensions must match: $(a\times b)(b\times c)$ produces $a\times c$. Numbers in these displays are rounded to six significant digits for readability; calculations and verification use the full precision values. ## 1. What does fitting minimize? For a candidate $\beta$, fitted values are $X\beta$ and residuals are $r=y-X\beta$. The residual sum of squares is $$RSS(\beta)=r^\top r=\sum_i(y_i-x_i^\top\beta)^2.$$ OLS chooses $\hat\beta=\arg\min_\beta RSS(\beta)$. Squaring makes large errors costly and gives a smooth quadratic. Differentiating gives $-2X^\top(y-X\beta)$; at the minimum, $$X^\top X\hat\beta=X^\top y.$$ These normal equations explain the answer. Computing $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ directly is a poor numerical strategy: forming $X^\top X$ squares the condition number. The implementation solves through SVD instead. ::: {#273e6a1d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def rss_at(beta): residuals = y - X @ np.asarray(beta) return residuals @ residuals print("RSS at generating coefficients [650, 18]:", rss_at([650, 18])) print("Gradient there:", -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ np.array([650, 18]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RSS at generating coefficients [650, 18]: 264940.4373000001 Gradient there: [ 847.18 32810.806] ``` ::: ::: At the trial coefficients $\beta=[650,18]^\top$, each fitted outcome is $1\cdot650+\mathrm{area}_i\cdot18$. The residual is the observed outcome minus that fit. ::: {#cf8a7091 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} trial_beta = np.array([650., 18.]) show_matrix(r"\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", trial_beta) show_matrix(r"X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", X @ trial_beta) show_matrix(r"y-X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", y - X @ trial_beta) show_matrix(r"X^\top X", X.T @ X) show_matrix(r"X^\top y", X.T @ y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle \beta_{\mathrm{trial}} = \begin{bmatrix}650 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}} = \begin{bmatrix}1989.2 \\ 1683.2 \\ 1845.2 \\ 1533.8 \\ 1472.6 \\ 2313.2 \\ 1316 \\ 2340.2\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle y-X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}} = \begin{bmatrix}-109.95 \\ 121.83 \\ 177.09 \\ -265.95 \\ 36.64 \\ -73.1 \\ -356.49 \\ 46.34\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix}8 & 516.3 \\ 516.3 & 36462.4\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle X^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}14069.8 \\ 975512\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)$ ::: ::: Here $X^\top X$ has dimensions $(2\times8)(8\times2)=2\times2$. Its top-left entry is the sum of eight squared ones, hence 8; its top-right entry is the sum of the observed floor areas; its bottom-right entry is the sum of their squares. For example, its top-right calculation begins $1\cdot74.4+1\cdot57.4+\cdots+1\cdot93.9$. $X^\top y$ contains the sum of rents and the sum of area–rent products. The normal equations give two equations for the two unknown coefficients. We show these products to understand the mathematics; the numerical solver below uses SVD rather than the normal equations. ### Expand the dot products Every entry in a matrix product is one row–column dot product. Below, we show the first two and last terms of long sums; $\cdots$ stands for the omitted terms. **The result includes all eight observations**, not just the displayed terms. Both factors and results are rounded for display, so the equals sign describes the operation and $\approx$ marks the displayed numerical result. ::: {#96b5c01b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} for i in range(p): for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"(X^\top X)_{{{i+1},{j+1}}}", X[:, i], X[:, j]) for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"(X^\top y)_{{{j+1}}}", X[:, j], y) show_dot(r"(X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}})_1", X[0], trial_beta) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top X)_{1,1} = (1)\cdot(1) + (1)\cdot(1) + \cdots + (1)\cdot(1)\approx 8$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top X)_{1,2} = (1)\cdot(74.4) + (1)\cdot(57.4) + \cdots + (1)\cdot(93.9)\approx 516.3$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top X)_{2,1} = (74.4)\cdot(1) + (57.4)\cdot(1) + \cdots + (93.9)\cdot(1)\approx 516.3$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top X)_{2,2} = (74.4)\cdot(74.4) + (57.4)\cdot(57.4) + \cdots + (93.9)\cdot(93.9)\approx 36462.35$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top y)_{1} = (1)\cdot(1879.25) + (1)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (1)\cdot(2386.54)\approx 14069.81$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X^\top y)_{2} = (74.4)\cdot(1879.25) + (57.4)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (93.9)\cdot(2386.54)\approx 975511.9$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}})_1 = (1)\cdot(650) + (74.4)\cdot(18)\approx 1989.2$ ::: ::: The subscripts here use mathematical indexing starting at 1 (Python indices start at 0). In particular, $(X^\top X)_{1,2}$ and $(X^\top X)_{2,1}$ are equal: swapping the two factors in every scalar product does not change their sum. This is why $X^\top X$ is symmetric. ## 2. SVD gives a stable solution and a rank check ### What problem does SVD help us understand? **SVD means singular value decomposition.** A decomposition rewrites one matrix as a product of simpler matrices. It does not change the data or guess the coefficients. For our model, multiplying $X\beta$ takes two coefficient values and produces eight fitted rents. That is a map from a two-dimensional coefficient space into an eight-dimensional observation space. The possible fitted vectors form the **column space** of $X$: all linear combinations of its intercept and area columns. It is a two-dimensional plane through the origin inside that eight-dimensional space. The observed $y$ will generally lie outside this plane because it includes noise. Least squares seeks the point on the plane closest to $y$ in squared Euclidean distance. These are spaces of vectors, not a scatterplot of area against rent: the eight coordinates of an observation-space vector correspond to the eight apartments. ### Why scale the columns first? Scale the columns with $D=\operatorname{diag}(\|X_j\|)$, so $A=XD^{-1}$. Decompose $A=USV^\top$. Then $$\hat\beta=D^{-1}VS^{-1}U^\top y.$$ The notation $\|X_j\|=\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}$ is the Euclidean length of column $j$. $D$ has those lengths on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by $D^{-1}$ divides each column by its length, giving unit-length columns in $A$. This is column scaling, **not centering or z-score standardization**. The intercept column is scaled too; no observations are changed or removed. Define scaled coefficients $\theta=D\beta$. Then $A\theta=X\beta$, so this change of units preserves every possible fitted vector. We solve for $\theta$ and recover $\beta=D^{-1}\theta$. Scaling prevents the numerical rank decision from being dominated simply by the choice of metres versus centimetres. ### What do U, S and V mean? For our full-rank design, the thin SVD is $$A=USV^\top,\qquad U^\top U=I_2,\qquad V^\top V=VV^\top=I_2.$$ $I_2$ is the $2\times2$ identity matrix: ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. **Orthonormal** columns have length one and are perpendicular to one another; their dot products are therefore 1 with themselves and 0 with each other. Those equalities are exactly what the identity matrices say. | Matrix | Dimensions | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | $V$ | $2\times2$ | Its columns $v_j$ are orthonormal directions in scaled coefficient space. $V^\top$ expresses a coefficient vector in those directions. | | $S$ | $2\times2$ | Diagonal entries $s_j\ge0$ are singular values: the amount that $A$ stretches each corresponding direction. | | $U$ | $8\times2$ | Its columns $u_j$ are orthonormal directions spanning the possible fitted outcomes. | The key relationship for each direction is $$A v_j=s_j u_j.$$ So an input direction $v_j$ of length one becomes an output direction $u_j$ stretched to length $s_j$. Reading $A\theta=USV^\top\theta$ right to left: change coordinates using $V^\top$, scale them using $S$, and combine the observation-space directions using $U$. $V^\top$ is a rotation or reflection; the rectangular $U$ embeds two coordinates into the eight-dimensional fitted plane. The thin $U$ is not an invertible $8\times8$ rotation. Singular values are **not regression coefficients or error standard deviations**. They describe the design matrix, independent of the observed rents $y$. If a singular value is numerically zero, at least one coefficient cannot be uniquely identified. We reject the design. The threshold is $\epsilon\max(n,p)s_{max}$. Scaling makes this decision less dependent on predictor units. The Rust code calls nalgebra's `svd.solve()` for the scaled solution, then undoes the column scaling. ::: {#030bbe73 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} scales = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0) A = X / scales U, singular_values, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False) tolerance = np.finfo(float).eps * max(n, p) * singular_values[0] assert np.all(singular_values > tolerance) beta = (Vt.T @ ((U.T @ y) / singular_values)) / scales print("Singular values:", singular_values) print("Rank threshold:", tolerance) print("Coefficients:", beta) print("Normal-equation gradient (approximately zero):", -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ beta)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Singular values: [1.39855253 0.20988288] Rank threshold: 2.4843283507592642e-15 Coefficients: [372.47854453 21.47972428] Normal-equation gradient (approximately zero): [-2.27373675e-12 -1.54490355e-10] ``` ::: ::: The thin SVD keeps only the $p=2$ needed columns of $U$. Here $U$ is $8\times2$, $S$ is $2\times2$, and $V^\top$ is $2\times2$. $S$ is diagonal: its only nonzero entries are the singular values. $D^{-1}$ undoes the original column scaling. ::: {#b8d8d645 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} D = np.diag(scales) D_inverse = np.diag(1 / scales) S = np.diag(singular_values) show_matrix("D", D) show_matrix(r"D^{-1}", D_inverse) show_matrix(r"A=XD^{-1}", A) show_matrix("U", U) show_matrix("S", S) show_matrix(r"V^\top", Vt) show_matrix(r"U^\top y", U.T @ y) show_matrix(r"S^{-1}U^\top y", (U.T @ y) / singular_values) show_matrix(r"VS^{-1}U^\top y", Vt.T @ ((U.T @ y) / singular_values)) show_matrix(r"\hat\beta=D^{-1}VS^{-1}U^\top y", beta) np.testing.assert_allclose(U @ S @ Vt, A, atol=1e-14) np.testing.assert_allclose(X.T @ X @ beta, X.T @ y, atol=1e-8, rtol=1e-12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle D = \begin{bmatrix}2.82843 & 0 \\ 0 & 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle A=XD^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}0.353553 & 0.389628 \\ 0.353553 & 0.3006 \\ 0.353553 & 0.347733 \\ 0.353553 & 0.257134 \\ 0.353553 & 0.239328 \\ 0.353553 & 0.483893 \\ 0.353553 & 0.193767 \\ 0.353553 & 0.491749\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} \\ -0.427384 & 0.465588\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle S = \begin{bmatrix}1.39855 & 0 \\ 0 & execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} show_matrix(r"U^\top U", U.T @ U) show_matrix(r"V^\top V", Vt @ Vt.T) show_matrix(r"Av_1", A @ Vt.T[:, 0]) show_matrix(r"s_1u_1", singular_values[0] * U[:, 0]) np.testing.assert_allclose(U.T @ U, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14) np.testing.assert_allclose(Vt @ Vt.T, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14) np.testing.assert_allclose(A @ Vt.T[:, 0], singular_values[0] * U[:, 0], atol=1e-14) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle U^\top U = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1.40929e-17 \\ 1.40929e-17 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle V^\top V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle Av_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle s_1u_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: ### Derive the least-squares solution from the decomposition First project the outcomes onto the columns of $U$: $$c=U^\top y,\qquad y_\parallel=Uc,\qquad y_\perp=y-Uc.$$ Each $c_j=u_j^\top y$ is a dot product measuring how much of $y$ lies along direction $u_j$. $y_\parallel$ lies in the fitted plane, while $y_\perp$ is perpendicular to it. The model can fit the first part; no choice of coefficients can reproduce the second part. This is a geometric decomposition of the observed sample, not recovery of the true simulation errors. Write $z=V^\top\theta$. Because the two residual components are perpendicular, the Pythagorean theorem gives $$\|y-A\theta\|^2 =\|c-Sz\|^2+\|y_\perp\|^2.$$ The second term cannot change as we vary coefficients. The first term is minimized at zero by setting $z_j=c_j/s_j$. Thus $$\hat z=S^{-1}U^\top y,\qquad \hat\theta=V\hat z,\qquad \hat\beta=D^{-1}\hat\theta.$$ This explains the solution formula rather than just prescribing a sequence of matrix multiplications. It also gives $\hat y=UU^\top y$ and $r=y-UU^\top y$. $UU^\top$ is a projection matrix, not the $8\times8$ identity: it preserves vectors in the fitted plane and removes perpendicular components. There are two fitted directions and six residual directions, which is where $n-p=8-2=6$ comes from. ::: {#7305fbc3 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} coordinates = U.T @ y projected_y = U @ coordinates perpendicular_y = y - projected_y show_matrix(r"c=U^\top y", coordinates) show_matrix(r"y_\parallel=Uc", projected_y) show_matrix(r"y_\perp=y-Uc", perpendicular_y) show_matrix(r"U^\top y_\perp", U.T @ perpendicular_y) np.testing.assert_allclose(projected_y, X @ beta, atol=1e-10) np.testing.assert_allclose(U.T @ perpendicular_y, np.zeros(p), atol=1e-10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle c=U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}-5098.02 \\ 452.36\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle y_\parallel=Uc = \begin{bmatrix}1970.57 \\ 1605.41 \\ 1798.73 \\ 1427.13 \\ 1354.1 \\ 2357.21 \\ 1167.23 \\ 2389.42\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle y_\perp=y-Uc = \begin{bmatrix}-91.32 \\ 199.615 \\ 223.558 \\ -159.283 \\ 155.138 \\ -117.105 \\ -207.718 \\ -2.88465\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle U^\top y_\perp = \begin{bmatrix}8.19167e-13 \\ -2.69876e-14\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)$ ::: ::: Reading the final product from right to left: $U^\top y$ expresses the outcome in the left singular-vector directions; $S^{-1}$ divides by the singular values; $V$ converts back to scaled coefficient coordinates; $D^{-1}$ restores the original predictor units. Each intermediate coefficient vector is $2\times1$. The signs of corresponding singular vectors can differ across software while giving the same reconstructed matrix and coefficients. ::: {#b9126adc .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"(U^\top y)_{{{j+1}}}", U[:, j], y) scaled_coordinates = (U.T @ y) / singular_values for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"(VS^{-1}U^\top y)_{{{j+1}}}", Vt.T[j], scaled_coordinates) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (U^\top y)_{1} = (-0.37575198)\cdot(1879.25) + (-0.33073952)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (-0.42738393)\cdot(2386.54)\approx -5098.0192$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (U^\top y)_{2} = (0.12153867)\cdot(1879.25) + (-0.17840147)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (0.46558765)\cdot(2386.54)\approx 452.35992$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (VS^-1U^\top y)_{1} = (-0.70710678)\cdot(-3645.2111) + (-0.70710678)\cdot(2155.2969)\approx 1053.5284$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle (VS^-1U^\top y)_{2} = (-0.70710678)\cdot(-3645.2111) + (0.70710678)\cdot(2155.2969)\approx 4101.5785$ ::: ::: $S^{-1}$ and $D^{-1}$ are diagonal, so multiplying by them simply divides each coordinate by its corresponding singular value or column scale. ### Why small singular values matter If $s_j=0$, then $Av_j=0$: moving the coefficients along that nonzero direction does not change any fitted outcome. The data cannot distinguish those coefficient choices. For example, adding a second copy of area lets one area coefficient increase while the other decreases by the same amount. Only their sum matters. If $s_j$ is small but positive, division by $s_j$ amplifies changes in the outcome coordinates. The design is identifiable but coefficients can be sensitive to noise. The condition number $\kappa(A)=s_{\max}/s_{\min}$ measures that sensitivity in the scaled coordinates. Strongly correlated predictors often produce small singular values; full rank alone does not guarantee precise estimates. ::: {#48d8f6da .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Condition number of scaled design:", singular_values[0] / singular_values[-1]) duplicated = np.column_stack([X, X[:, 1]]) duplicated_scaled = duplicated / np.linalg.norm(duplicated, axis=0) duplicate_singular_values = np.linalg.svd(duplicated_scaled, compute_uv=False) duplicate_threshold = (np.finfo(float).eps * max(duplicated.shape) * duplicate_singular_values[0]) show_matrix(r"\text{singular values with duplicated area}", duplicate_singular_values) print("Smallest value:", duplicate_singular_values[-1]) print("Numerical rank threshold:", duplicate_threshold) assert duplicate_singular_values[-1] <= duplicate_threshold ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Condition number of scaled design: 6.663490322078895 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $\displaystyle \text{singular values with duplicated area} = \begin{bmatrix}1.71506 \\ 0.242043 \\ 1.62057e-17\end{bmatrix}\quad(3\times 1)$ ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Smallest value: 1.620565314202345e-17 Numerical rank threshold: 3.0465504588638278e-15 ``` ::: ::: In floating-point arithmetic, an exact zero may appear as a tiny positive number. Our threshold treats such directions as numerically rank deficient and rejects the fit with a clear error. It does not silently discard a predictor or divide by a nearly zero value. Finally, $A^\top A=VS^2V^\top$, so forming the normal-equation matrix squares the singular values and its condition number is $\kappa(A)^2$. This can lose accuracy before a solve even begins. SVD works with $A$ directly and exposes its rank. It avoids that extra numerical damage; it cannot make redundant predictors identifiable or make noisy data informative. ## 3. Residuals and degrees of freedom Full rank means we estimate $p$ coefficients, leaving $n-p$ independent residual directions. The unbiased variance estimate is $$s^2=\frac{RSS}{n-p},\qquad s=\sqrt{s^2}.$$ The result fields are `fitted`, `residuals`, `rss`, `df_residual`, `residual_variance`, and `sigma`. Covariance, standard errors and t-tests Under independent errors with constant variance, $$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=s^2(X^\top X)^{-1} =s^2D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}.$$ The code computes the latter expression, without forming $X^\top X$. Standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal. Under Gaussian errors, $(\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/SE_j$ has a Student t distribution with $n-p$ degrees of freedom. For $H_0:\beta_j=0$, the statistic is $t_j=\hat\beta_j/SE_j$, the two-sided p-value is $2P(T\ge |t_j|)$, and the 95% interval is $\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,n-p}SE_j$. Use the survival function for upper tails to avoid subtracting a CDF close to one. These are conventional homoskedastic standard errors, not robust estimates. For the fixed 95% interval, Rust finds the critical value by bisection on $P(T>t)=0.025$. Large-sample checks found that statrs' inverse-beta quantile lost precision at high residual degrees of freedom. Solving on the survival function preserves agreement with R; this notebook independently uses SciPy's `t.ppf`. See the [large-data report](../benchmarks/ols.qmd) and the focused Rust critical-value test for the regression evidence. ::: {#f58a2dda .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} scaled_inverse = (Vt.T / singular_values) @ (Vt / singular_values[:, None]) covariance = variance * scaled_inverse / scales[:, None] / scales[None, :] se = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance)) t_statistics = beta / se p_values = 2 * t.sf(np.abs(t_statistics), df) critical = t.ppf(0.975, df) conf_int = np.column_stack([beta - critical * se, beta + critical * se]) display(pd.DataFrame(covariance, index=["intercept", "area_m2"], columns=["intercept", "area_m2"])) display(pd.DataFrame({"coefficient": beta, "SE": se, "t": t_statistics, "p": p_values, "lower 95%": conf_int[:, 0], "upper 95%": conf_int[:, 1]}, index=["intercept", "area_m2"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Taking the square root of each diagonal entry gives the $2\times1$ standard-error vector. The interval matrix has one row per coefficient and two columns: lower and upper bounds. ## 5. R-squared and the intercept convention With a column of exact ones, use $TSS=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$ and $R^2=1-RSS/TSS$. Adjusted R-squared is $1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-p)$. Without an intercept, use uncentered $TSS=\sum_i y_i^2$ and adjusted R-squared $1-(1-R^2)n/(n-p)$, matching R's no-intercept convention. Do not compare centered and uncentered R-squared as if they used the same baseline. ::: {#e1385594 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} has_intercept = bool(np.any(np.all(X == 1, axis=0))) tss = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2) if has_intercept else y @ y r_squared = 1 - rss / tss adj_r_squared = 1 - (1 - r_squared) * (n - int(has_intercept)) / df print(f"R²={r_squared:.9f}; adjusted R²={adj_r_squared:.9f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R²=0.876374351; adjusted R²=0.855770076 ``` ::: ::: ## 6. Gaussian likelihood explains the same estimator For independent $y_i\sim N(x_i^\top\beta,\sigma^2)$, multiply the normal densities and take logs: $$\ell(\beta,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{RSS(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}.$$ At fixed positive variance, maximizing this expression minimizes RSS, so it gives the same OLS coefficients. Differentiate with respect to $v=\sigma^2$: $$\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}=-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{RSS}{2v^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat v_{ML}=RSS/n.$$ This ML variance differs from $RSS/(n-p)$ used for standard errors. At the estimates, $$\ell(\hat\beta,\hat v_{ML})=-\frac n2[\log(2\pi)+\log(RSS/n)+1].$$ ::: {#ffc66d1b .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} ml_variance = rss / n log_likelihood = -n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(ml_variance) + 1) def log_likelihood_at(candidate, v): return -n / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * v) - rss_at(candidate) / (2 * v) print(f"ML variance={ml_variance:.8f}; inference variance={variance:.8f}") print(f"Log-likelihood={log_likelihood:.9f}") assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta + [0, 0.1], ml_variance) assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta, 2 * ml_variance) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ML variance=25558.92538208; inference variance=34078.56717611 Log-likelihood=-51.946475724 ``` ::: ::: ## 7. Cross-implementation agreement is evidence; it does not replace understanding the formulas. ::: {#4076ddc1 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} calculated = dict(coefficients=beta, covariance=covariance, std_errors=se, t_statistics=t_statistics, p_values=p_values, conf_int=conf_int, fitted=fitted, residuals=residuals, rss=rss, residual_variance=variance, sigma=sigma, r_squared=r_squared, adj_r_squared=adj_r_squared, df_residual=df, log_likelihood=log_likelihood) for key, value in calculated.items(): np.testing.assert_allclose(value, case["expected"][key], atol=1e-9, rtol=1e-7, err_msg=key) print("All displayed calculations agree with the committed R fixture.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All displayed calculations agree with the committed R fixture. ``` ::: ::: ## 8. Missing data, singularity and perfect fits The PHP call drops a whole row if any supplied predictor or its outcome is `null` or `NAN`, warns once on a successful fit, and reports original row positions. It applies all formulas above to the retained sample: $n$ and $n-p$ change. Use `missing: 'raise'` to reject missingness. Infinity, malformed values and rank failure remain errors. See [missing-data contract](../missing-data.qmd). Listwise deletion changes the estimation sample; it is not imputation and does not guarantee unbiased results when missingness is related to the outcome or predictors. Document why data are missing and which observations were retained. At exact zero RSS, standard errors are zero and the Gaussian log-likelihood has an infinite limit as variance approaches zero. A zero coefficient divided by a zero standard error is undefined (NaN); a nonzero coefficient gives infinite t and zero p. If TSS is also zero, R-squared is undefined. Decomposition roundoff can leave small residuals in mathematically perfect fits; unstable t-statistics and likelihoods should not be compared tightly across algorithms.
